b1plus-noun-clause-dik.title: Noun Clauses with -DIk (Knowing/Saying That...)
b1plus-noun-clause-dik.explanation: You already used -DIk to build relative clauses (the book [that] I read). The same participle, now carrying a possessive suffix to mark WHO does the action and a case suffix to mark its role in the sentence, turns a whole clause into a noun: 'Onun geldiğini biliyorum' (I know that he came/is coming) literally means 'I know his coming.' The same pattern extends naturally to the future with -EcEk instead of -DIk: 'Geleceğini biliyorum' (I know that he will come).
b1plus-noun-clause-dik.fact: A -DIk noun clause doesn't have a strict present/past split the way an English 'that'-clause does: geldiğini can mean 'that he came' or 'that he is coming' depending on context, since the participle marks realized fact, not a specific tense.

dialogue.tr: Onun bu işi bitirdiğini biliyor musun?
dialogue.en: Do you know that he finished this job?
Yes, I know, I heard that he worked a lot.

b1plus-noun-clause-ma.title: Noun Clauses with -mA (Wanting Someone to Do)
b1plus-noun-clause-ma.explanation: -DIk clauses report facts. -mA clauses express desires, requests, or actions that aren't (yet) real. istemek always takes -mA: 'Gitmemi istiyor' (He wants me to go) literally means 'he wants my going.' The same -mA nominal is used after asking/allowing/suggesting verbs (rica etmek, izin vermek, teklif etmek) and after postpositions like -DAn (hoşlanmak, korkmak) and -(y)A (başlamak, devam etmek).
b1plus-noun-clause-ma.fact: The choice between -DIk and -mA isn't about tense, it's about reality: -DIk marks something that happened or is a known fact, -mA marks something wanted, possible, or not-yet-real. 'Geldiğini biliyorum' (I know he came, a fact) vs 'Gelmesini istiyorum' (I want him to come, not yet real).

dialogue.en: What do you want from me?
I want you to come early.

b1plus-past-continuous.title: Past Continuous and Future-in-the-Past
b1plus-past-continuous.pattern: -Iyor + du (was doing); -EcEk + ti (was going to do)
b1plus-past-continuous.explanation: You know -Iyor (present continuous) and -EcEk (future). Add the past copula -DI to either and the whole frame shifts into the past: 'yapıyordum' (I was doing), 'yapacaktım' (I was going to do). A third related pattern, aorist + -DI, means 'used to': 'okurdum' (I used to read) describes a repeated past habit rather than a single moment in progress.
b1plus-past-continuous.fact: -EcEktI often carries the extra flavor of 'but it didn't happen': 'Gelecektim ama gelemedim' (I was going to come but I couldn't) — a broken plan, not just a neutral future-in-the-past.
